prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- British Prime Minister Gordon Brown's wife, Sarah, wore an outfit from designer Britt Lintner to greet President Obama and his wife, Michelle, while Michelle Obama wore J.Crew, according to spokeswomen for both sides. Sarah Brown, left, wears a dress from an American designer. Michelle Obama wears J.Crew. Both women later changed and wore other designer outfits for the formal pre-G-20 summit dinner at 10 Downing Street, the British prime minister's official residence. Wednesday morning, Sarah Brown wore a one-of-a-kind navy dress with red lining by the American-born Lintner, a spokeswoman for 10 Downing Street said. The designer specially made the dress in navy for Brown, but retails the garment in black for $720, Lintner said. Michelle Obama's outfit included a $158 green skirt and $298 bead and rhinestone cardigan from J.Crew, the store's Web site showed. Brown also wore a pair of Astley Clarke earrings, according to a spokeswoman from 10 Downing Street. The Astley Clarke Web site sells earrings from less than $100 to more than $10,000. The first ladies' choices of outfits during this summit are being closely watched by the world's media, both in terms of style and comparative cost. Both women pay for all of their clothes themselves and receive no clothing allowance, according to spokeswomen for both sides. Lintner first designed a dress for Brown for the British Fashion Council Awards in November 2007, Lintner said. She sells to clients only through her West London studio and said she started her company out of frustration over the selection of workwear available for women. Although the clothes are expensive, she said, they are made to last. This is not the first time Michelle Obama has chosen an "off the rack" outfit. She has worn J.Crew before, including in American Vogue. When appearing on "The Tonight Show" with Jay Leno, she wore a J.Crew ensemble, on which she commented, "You get some good stuff online." After the photo call, Obama and Brown visited Maggie's Cancer Caring Center, where Brown is a patron. The spouses of the G-20 leaders have several events scheduled during their stay in London. On Tuesday, Brown will be host of a dinner for G-20 spouses. The dinner will take place at No. 11 Downing Street, the London residence of the chancellor of the exchequer, while the G-20 leaders take a working dinner next door at No. 10. As well as the spouses of the G-20 leaders, prominent women in British sport, arts, fashion, charity and business are also expected to attend. Downing Street has said those invited are "all intended to show off British talent." Those invited include "Harry Potter" author J.K. Rowling, supermodel Naomi Campbell and Olympic gold medal runner Kelly Holmes. Downing Street sources said Michelle Obama will be seated between Holmes and Rowling. The spouses also will visit the Royal Opera House in Covent Garden, London. They are expected to watch some short performances of opera and ballet, the Prime Minister's Press Office said.

LONDON, England (CNN) — Fashion choices drew attention as Sarah Brown, wife of British Prime Minister Gordon Brown, welcomed President Barack Obama and first lady Michelle Obama. Representatives for both women said Brown chose a Britt Lintner design, while Obama appeared in clothing from J.Crew.

For Wednesday morning’s welcome, Brown wore a unique navy-blue dress with red lining created by Lintner, an American-born designer, according to a 10 Downing Street spokeswoman. Lintner said the navy version had been made specifically for Brown. A black version of the same garment is sold for $720. Brown completed her look with Astley Clarke earrings, Downing Street said. Earrings listed on the Astley Clarke website range in price from under $100 to more than $10,000.

Obama’s J.Crew ensemble consisted of a green skirt priced at $158 and a cardigan decorated with beads and rhinestones costing $298, according to the retailer’s website.

Later, both women changed into clothes by other designers for the formal dinner held ahead of the G-20 summit at 10 Downing Street, the British prime minister’s official home.

International media closely followed the two women’s summit wardrobes, comparing both their style and cost. Spokeswomen for each side said Brown and Obama purchase their own clothing and are not provided with wardrobe allowances.

Lintner’s relationship with Brown dates to November 2007, when she first created a dress for her to wear to the British Fashion Council Awards. Lintner sells directly to customers only from her studio in West London. She said she founded her business because she was dissatisfied with the workwear options available to women. Although her pieces carry high prices, she said they are designed for long-term use.

Obama, meanwhile, has previously selected ready-to-wear clothing. She has worn J.Crew on other occasions, including for American Vogue. During an appearance on “The Tonight Show” with Jay Leno, she also dressed in a J.Crew outfit and remarked, “You get some good stuff online.”

Following the photo opportunity, Brown and Obama went to Maggie’s Cancer Caring Center, an organization of which Brown is a patron.

A number of activities were arranged for the spouses of G-20 leaders during their time in London. On Tuesday, Brown was scheduled to host a dinner for them at No. 11 Downing Street, the London home of the chancellor of the exchequer. At the same time, the G-20 leaders were to attend a working dinner next door at No. 10.

The guest list was expected to include not only the leaders’ spouses but also notable British women from business, charity, fashion, the arts and sport. Downing Street said all the invitees were chosen to “show off British talent.” Among them were “Harry Potter” writer J.K. Rowling, supermodel Naomi Campbell and Olympic gold medal-winning runner Kelly Holmes. Sources at Downing Street said Michelle Obama would sit between Rowling and Holmes.

The spouses were also due to visit London’s Royal Opera House in Covent Garden, where they were expected to see brief ballet and opera performances, according to the Prime Minister’s Press Office.

# High-low diplomacy: Michelle Obama and Sarah Brown put fashion in the G-20 spotlight

**London, England (CNN)** — While their husbands confronted a deepening global economic crisis at the G-20 summit, Michelle Obama and Sarah Brown pursued a softer form of diplomacy — with visits to schools, cultural institutions and charities, and wardrobes closely watched on both sides of the Atlantic.

Obama arrived at 10 Downing Street in an outfit from American retailer J.Crew, pairing a pale green pencil skirt with an embellished cream cardigan. At the time, the cardigan retailed for about **$298** and the skirt for roughly **$158**, giving the ensemble a combined price of approximately **$456**, before shoes and accessories.

The choice reinforced the first lady’s reputation for mixing accessible brands with high-end designers. During the London visit, she also wore pieces by **Jason Wu**, the designer of her inaugural ball gown, and Cuban-born American designer **Isabel Toledo**. Published estimates placed Wu’s custom dresses in the several-thousand-dollar range, although exact prices for Obama’s made-to-measure outfits were not released.

Brown, the wife of British Prime Minister Gordon Brown, emphasized British fashion, wearing outfits associated with designers including **Graeme Black** and **Britt Lintner**. Her office did not disclose what she paid, and custom garments do not always carry a public retail price; comparable dresses by those designers were reported at the time to cost several hundred pounds, with some approaching or exceeding **£1,000**.

The contrast was politically appealing during a summit focused on recession and unemployment: Obama’s widely available J.Crew separates offered a high-street message, while Brown’s selections promoted British design.

Fashion, however, was only one part of the spouses’ schedule. Sarah Brown hosted the visiting leaders’ partners for a program that included cultural and charitable events, among them a visit to the **Royal Opera House** and a stop at a **Maggie’s cancer-support center** in west London.

Michelle Obama also made a separate visit to the **Elizabeth Garrett Anderson School** in north London, where she spoke to students about education, ambition and her own upbringing. The appearance became one of the most memorable moments of her first overseas trip as first lady.

Meanwhile, President Barack Obama and Prime Minister Gordon Brown joined other G-20 leaders for negotiations centered on restoring economic growth, strengthening financial regulation and helping developing nations withstand the global downturn.

For the first ladies, the London summit offered a parallel stage — one where diplomacy was conducted through public appearances, charitable causes and carefully chosen clothes.

## Sarah Brown Goes Bespoke as Michelle Obama Champions J.Crew

Sarah Brown and Michelle Obama offered a study in contrasting approaches to political style during their visit to Maggie’s Cancer Caring Center in west London: one chose a custom-made British dress, while the other turned to an accessible American high-street favorite.

Brown wore a dress created especially for her by London-based designer Britt Lintner. The polished, understated design reflected Brown’s preference for discreet British fashion, with its tailored silhouette and restrained palette allowing the workmanship—not a prominent label—to take center stage. The choice also gave valuable exposure to a less internationally familiar British name at a moment of intense global attention.

Obama, meanwhile, continued her much-discussed habit of mixing prestige fashion with affordable pieces. The first lady appeared in an off-the-rack J.Crew ensemble, pairing a softly colored skirt with a decorative cardigan and simple layers. Rather than commissioning a one-off outfit for the engagement, she selected clothes available to ordinary shoppers, reinforcing the democratic, approachable image that has become central to her fashion identity.

Together, the two looks neatly captured the women’s different style strategies. Brown’s bespoke Britt Lintner dress served as a quiet endorsement of British design and traditional tailoring. Obama’s J.Crew outfit delivered a more populist message, demonstrating that a first lady could look polished on the international stage without relying exclusively on couture.

Fashion, however, remained secondary to the purpose of the visit. At Maggie’s Cancer Caring Center, Brown and Obama met patients, families and staff and learned more about the organization’s work providing practical, emotional and social support to people affected by cancer. Their warm exchanges brought a personal dimension to a diplomatic schedule otherwise dominated by the high-level meetings surrounding the London summit.

Attention was also turning to the upcoming dinner at 10 Downing Street, where Brown was due to host Obama and other guests. The evening engagement promised another round of sartorial scrutiny, with observers eager to see whether Brown would continue promoting British talent and whether Obama would retain her signature mix of designer pieces and attainable American fashion.

For the daytime appearance, at least, the contrast was clear: Brown made the case for bespoke British elegance, while Obama showed the global appeal of off-the-rack J.Crew.

As world leaders gather for the G-20 summit, part of the media’s attention has shifted from economic policy to the wardrobes of Michelle Obama and Sarah Brown.

Newspapers and broadcasters have closely followed the two women’s choices of dresses, coats and accessories, often presenting their appearances as a meeting of American and British style. But aides have emphasized that neither wardrobe is being financed by taxpayers: both Mrs. Obama and Mrs. Brown pay for their own clothing.

The fashion coverage is likely to continue as the leaders’ spouses take part in a separate program intended to showcase British culture and hospitality. Plans include receptions, a visit to the Royal Opera House and opportunities to meet performers and representatives of the arts. The spouses are also expected to attend social events connected with the summit, including a dinner bringing together the visiting delegations.

The cultural itinerary offers a less formal counterpart to the leaders’ discussions on the global economy. Although cameras will inevitably focus on what the first ladies are wearing, the planned events are designed to draw attention to Britain’s artistic institutions and to give the spouses time to meet away from the summit’s negotiating rooms.
